intro: Enter a, b and c for ax² + bx + c = 0 and get the roots, the discriminant, the vertex and the axis of symmetry. When the roots are rational you also get the factored form.

formula.label: Discriminant
formula.note: D positive: two real roots. D = 0: one repeated root. D negative: two complex roots.

howItWorks: First the solver works out the discriminant, b² − 4ac. This one number tells you what kind of answer to expect. If it is positive there are two different real roots, if it is 0 there is one repeated root, and if it is negative the roots are complex numbers that use i, where i² = −1.

Next it puts a, b and the discriminant into the quadratic formula and shows each step. The vertex is the turning point of the curve y = ax² + bx + c. Its x value is −b ÷ (2a), and the axis of symmetry is the vertical line through it.

If the roots are whole numbers or fractions, the equation can also be written in factored form, such as 2(x − 3)(x + 1). This is a quick way to check the roots, because each bracket is zero at one of them.

example.title: Two real roots
steps: Read off the values: a = 2, b = −4, c = −6.
Discriminant: D = (−4)² − 4 × 2 × (−6) = 16 + 48 = 64. It is positive, so there are two real roots.
Vertex: x = −(−4) ÷ (2 × 2) = 1, and y = 2(1)² − 4(1) − 6 = −8. The axis of symmetry is x = 1.
example.answer: x = 3 or x = −1, vertex (1, −8), factored form 2(x − 3)(x + 1).

mistakes.title: Squaring a negative b wrongly
mistakes.text: If b = −4, then b² = (−4)² = 16, not −16. A negative number squared is always positive.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the minus in −b
mistakes.text: The formula starts with −b. When b = −4, −b is +4, so the top becomes 4 ± √D.

mistakes.title: Dividing only the square root by 2a
mistakes.text: The whole top, −b ± √D, is divided by 2a. For the example, (4 + 8) ÷ 4 = 3, not 4 + 8 ÷ 4 = 6.

mistakes.title: Not rearranging to = 0 first
mistakes.text: For x² = 5x − 6, move everything to one side first: x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Only then is a = 1, b = −5 and c = 6, giving roots 2 and 3.

faqs.q: What does the discriminant tell me?
faqs.a: It tells you how many real roots there are. Positive means two, zero means one repeated root, and negative means no real roots but two complex ones.
They are roots that use i, the number whose square is −1. For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, D = 4 − 20 = −16, so the roots are x = −1 + 2i and x = −1 − 2i.
If a = 0, the x² term disappears and you are left with a linear equation like bx + c = 0. That is not a quadratic, and the formula would mean dividing by zero.

faqs.q: What does the vertex mean on a graph?
faqs.a: It is the turning point of the curve. If a is positive the curve opens upwards and the vertex is the lowest point; if a is negative it is the highest point.

faqs.q: Why is there no factored form for some equations?
faqs.a: The factored form is shown only when the roots are rational, meaning whole numbers or fractions. For x² − 2 = 0 the roots are ±√2, which are not fractions, so there is no neat factored form with rational numbers.
